claims.evidence: Supported by multispectral immunofluorescence staining data.

claims.claim: Only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules.
claims.source: only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules that possibly regulated by RET
claims.evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data and immunohistochemistry staining.

claims.claim: HLA-I downregulation in kinase-type PCCs is possibly regulated by RET.
claims.source: only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules that possibly regulated by RET
claims.evidence: Inferred from the co-occurrence of RET expression and HLA-I downregulation, and supported by prior literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I.

claims.claim: Kinase-type PCCs have potential for combined therapy with kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy.
claims.source: suggesting the potential of combined therapy with kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy for kinase-type PCCs
claims.evidence: Speculative claim based on the observed HLA-I downregulation and RET expression patterns.

claims.claim: The application of immunotherapy to metabolism-type PCCs is likely unsuitable.
claims.source: in contrast, the application of immunotherapy to metabolism-type PCCs (with antigen presentation ability) is likely unsuitable.
claims.evidence: Speculative claim based on the lack of CD8+ T cell infiltration despite antigen presentation ability.

claims.claim: 133,894 individual cells were retained after quality control filtering.
claims.source: After quality control filtering to remove cells with low gene detection and high mitochondrial gene coverage, we retained 133,894 individual cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data processing and quality control metrics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–2C.

claims.claim: 13 cell types were identified in the PCC microenvironment including adrenal cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, T cells, natural killer cells, proliferating cells, plasma cells, B cells, mast cells, and sustentacular cells.
claims.source: We classified the 67 detected clusters into 13 cell types according to their expression profiles for recognized marker genes and Spearman correlation analysis between clusters: the classified cell types included adrenal cells (marked by DLK1 and RBP1), endothelial cells (marked by PECAM1 and VWF), fibroblasts (marked by THY1 and PLAC9), smooth muscle cells (marked by ACTA2 and TAGLN), monocytes/macrophages (marked by CD14 and CD163), neutrophils (marked by S100A8 and S100A9), T cells (marked by IL7R and CD3D), natural killer cells (NKs, marked by KLRD1 and GNLY), proliferating cells (marked by TOP2A and MKI67), plasma cells (marked by XBP1 and IGKC), B cells (marked by MS4A1 and CD79A), mast cells (marked by KIT and TPSB2), and sustentacular cells (marked by S100B and CRYAB) (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by marker gene expression analysis and visualization in Figures 1C, 1D, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The PASS scores of 11 collected PCC tissues ranged from 2 to 9.
claims.source: The PASS scores of 11 collected PCC tissues ranged from 2 to 9, showing obvious heterogeneity among the examined intra-tumoral sites and inter-individual comparisons for the 5 PCC patients (Supplementary file 1b).
claims.evidence: Supported by PASS scoring data in Supplementary file 1b.

claims.claim: P4 showed low correlation with the other three sporadic PCCs patients (P1-P3).
claims.source: The inter-individual correlation analysis indicated that P4 showed low correlation with the other three sporadic PCCs patients (P1-P3) (Figure 2C)
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: P4 had a significantly elevated proportion of adrenal cells (77%) compared to P1-P3 (16-36%).
claims.source: and further analysis of cell type fractions showed a significantly elevated proportion of adrenal cells (77%) in P4; the adrenal cells comprised between 16 and 36% of the total cells in the P1-P3 specimens (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: P5 had a higher proportion of endothelial cells (35%) compared to P1-P4 (3–10%).
claims.source: reflecting a higher proportion of endothelial cells in P5 (35%) as compared to P1-P4 (3–10%) (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: VHL syndrome is associated with vascular endothelial hyperplasia.
claims.source: Consistent with the reported vascular endothelial hyperplasia phenotype in VHL syndrome (Vortmeyer et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Vortmeyer et al., 2013).

claims.claim: CopyKAT algorithm distinguishes PCC cells from normal chromaffin cells based on genomic copy number variants.
claims.source: The copy number karyotyping of aneuploid tumors (CopyKAT) algorithm (Gao et al., 2021) was applied, which estimates genomic copy number variants (CNVs) from scRNA-seq data by employing an integrative Bayesian segmentation approach to distinguish PCC cells from normal chromaffin cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to the CopyKAT method (Gao et al., 2021) and its application to the scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Inferred aneuploid tumor cells highly expressed Chromogranin B (CHGB), which is a marker of PCC cells.
claims.source: Consistently, the inferred aneuploid tumor cells highly expressed Chromogranin B (CHGB), which is a marker of PCC cells (Wiedenmann et al., 1988; Winkler and Fischer-Colbrie, 1992; Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B and C, and citations to prior literature (Wiedenmann et al., 1988; Winkler and Fischer-Colbrie, 1992).

claims.claim: Two CNV patterns were identified among the inferred aneuploid tumor cells, with distinctions evident in chromosomes 3, 11, and 17.
claims.source: We noticed two CNV patterns among the inferred aneuploid tumor cells, with the distinction evident in chromosomes 3, 11, and 17 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Cells in inferred tumor cluster A exhibited high expression of NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2.
claims.source: We observed that cells in inferred tumor cluster A exhibited high expression of NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis of tumor clusters.

claims.claim: Cells in inferred tumor cluster B expressed high levels of PNMT and RET.
claims.source: while cells in inferred tumor cluster B expressed high levels of PNMT and RET (Figure 3D and E)
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: PNMT is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine.
claims.source: PNMT is known as an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine
claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about PNMT function.

claims.claim: RET is a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family.
claims.source: and that RET is a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family
claims.evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about RET.

claims.claim: NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 function in the oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis pathways.
claims.source: while NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 respectively function in the oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis pathways (Drilon et al., 2018; Mahmoodi et al., 2020; Sinkler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drilon et al., 2018; Mahmoodi et al., 2020; Sinkler et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Tumor cluster A DEGs showed functional enrichment for terms including generation of metabolites and energy, response to oxygen levels, response to hypoxia, and ATP metabolic process.
claims.source: the tumor cluster A DEGs showed functional enrichment for terms including generation of metabolites and energy, response to oxygen levels, response to hypoxia, and ATP metabolic process and some notably upregulated genes of tumor cluster A included known energy metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, COX4I2, RGS4, and AQP1 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Tumor cluster B DEGs showed enrichment for terms including cytoplasmic translation, neuron projection development, axon development, and cell growth.
claims.source: For tumor cluster B, the GO analysis showed enrichment for terms including cytoplasmic translation, neuron projection development, axon development, and cell growth, and there was obvious upregulation of PNMT, RET, and genes encoding other kinases known to function in proliferation, as well as genes that participate in the regulation of neuroendocrine functions (e.g. CALM1, PENK, and NPY; Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Immunocytochemistry staining showed strong accumulation of PNMT and RET in P4.
claims.source: Notably, immunocytochemistry staining of serial tumor sections showed strong accumulation of PNMT and RET in P4
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 accumulation was characteristic for the P1-P3 and P5 sections.
claims.source: while NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 accumulation was characteristic for the P1-P3 and P5 sections, providing protein-level evidence to validate the differential trends detected from the scRNA-seq results (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: P4 exhibited relatively higher blood pressures and plasma levels of 3-methoxytyramine and normetanephrine compared to P1-P3 and P5.
claims.source: When considering clinical information from five PCC patients, including tumor size, signs, symptoms and laboratory tests, we observed that P4 exhibited relatively higher blood pressures and the plasma levels of 3-methoxytyramine and normetanephrine compared to P1-P3 and P5 (Supplementary file 1c)
claims.evidence: Supported by clinical data in Supplementary file 1c.

claims.claim: Late up-regulated genes in metabolism-type PCCs include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion.
claims.source: Late up-regulated genes include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion, which highly expressed in subcluster 2 (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C and established knowledge about S100A4 and TAGLN functions.

claims.claim: Metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, ATP5MG, NDUFB4, and COX17 were highly expressed at early stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
claims.source: Metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, ATP5MG, NDUFB4, and COX17 were highly expressed at early stage, while SOD3 and COX7A1 were up-regulated at the late stage (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 is highly expressed at early stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
claims.source: We also found the high expression of tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 at early stage and subsequent up-regulation of the oncogene JUNB (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Oncogene JUNB is up-regulated at late stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
claims.source: We also found the high expression of tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 at early stage and subsequent up-regulation of the oncogene JUNB (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: CALM1 and CALM2 are highly expressed early in kinase-type PCC cells.
claims.source: Further analysis of DEGs in the pseudotime trajectory showed early high expression of CALM1 and CALM2 in the subcluster 1, and late up-regulation of RET in the subcluster 2 (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: RET is up-regulated late in kinase-type PCC cells.
claims.source: Further analysis of DEGs in the pseudotime trajectory showed early high expression of CALM1 and CALM2 in the subcluster 1, and late up-regulation of RET in the subcluster 2 (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: PNMT is expressed early in kinase-type PCC cells.
claims.source: We also noticed the early expression of PNMT, while neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 were up-regulated later in the pseudotime trajectory (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 are up-regulated later in kinase-type PCC cells.
claims.source: We also noticed the early expression of PNMT, while neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 were up-regulated later in the pseudotime trajectory (Figure 5F)
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: PCC cells with high expression of RET exhibit neuron-like phenotypes.
claims.source: suggesting the decrease of epinephrine synthesis and the appearance of neuron-like phenotypes during tumor evolution, consistent with previously reported neuron-like phenotypes in PCC cells with high expression of RET (Califano et al., 1995; Powers et al., 2003; Powers et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Califano et al., 1995; Powers et al., 2003; Powers et al., 2009).

claims.claim: ANXA1-FPR1 pair is the major participant in the annexin signaling pathway in metabolism-type PCCs.
claims.source: Further analysis of participated ligand-receptors showed major participation of ANXA1-FPR1 pair in the annexin signaling pathway (Figure 6B)
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: ANXA1 and FPR1 are highly co-expressed in neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages.
claims.source: and high co-expression of ANXA1 and FPR1 in neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The annexin signaling pathway is activated under a strong inflammatory reaction.
claims.source: It has been reported that the annexin signaling pathway is known to be activated under a strong inflammatory reaction (Gastardelo et al., 2014; Gavins et al., 2003; Gerke and Moss, 2002; Hayhoe et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Gastardelo et al., 2014; Gavins et al., 2003; Gerke and Moss, 2002; Hayhoe et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Metabolism-type PCCs have a higher proportion of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages compared with kinase-type.
claims.source: Combined with our findings of a higher proportion of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages in metabolism-type as compared with kinase-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The inflammatory response signaling pathway showed enrichment in metabolism-type PCCs compared with kinase-type PCC.
claims.source: As expected, the inflammatory response signaling pathway showed enrichment in metabolism-type PCCs as compared with that in kinase-type PCC (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: VEGF signaling pathway is activated in P5 (VHL patient).
claims.source: We noticed the activation of VEGF signaling pathway in P5 (Figure 6E)
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs are major contributors to VEGF signaling pathway in P5.
claims.source: and major contribution of PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs to VEGF signaling pathway (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: VEGFA and VEGFR1 are highly expressed in tumor cells in P5.
claims.source: Specifically, VEGFA and VEGFR1 were highly expressed in tumor cells, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 in endothelial cells, and PLGF in fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 6G)
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: FGF1-FGFR1 is the major participant in the FGF pathway in kinase-type PCC.
claims.source: and identified the activation of FGF signaling network (Figure 6H) and major involvement of FGF1-FGFR1 in the FGF pathway (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6H and 6I.

claims.claim: Smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1 in kinase-type PCC.
claims.source: The smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1, while tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: Tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 in kinase-type PCC.
claims.source: The smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1, while tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: FGF1-FGFR1 pair regulates tumor cell proliferation.
claims.source: The analyses suggested the cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells through the FGF1-FGFR1 pair, which regulated the tumor cell proliferation (Katoh, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Katoh, 2016).

claims.claim: Kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors.
claims.source: These results indicate that kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors, which have been shown to exert inhibitory effects on tumor proliferation (Liang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Speculative claim based on FGF signaling activation and citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2012).

claims.claim: There is apparent crosstalk between tumor cells and T cells in metabolism-type patients.
claims.source: Visualization of inter-cellular communication showed apparent crosstalk between tumor cells and T cells in metabolism-type patients
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: There is a lack of apparent communication between tumor cells and T cells in the kinase-type patient.
claims.source: while we were surprised to find a lack of apparent communication between tumor cells and T cells in the kinase-type patient (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Kinase-type PCC cells could evade immune surveillance of T cells.
claims.source: These results suggested that kinase-type PCC cells could evade immune surveillance of T cells and further indicated the immune escape potential of kinase-type PCCs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of communication between tumor cells and T cells.

claims.claim: HLA-I surface level represents the antigen-presenting abilities of tumor cells.
claims.source: Considering leukocyte antigen-class I (HLA-I) surface level is known to represent the antigen-presenting abilities of tumor cells (Brea et al., 2016; Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Brea et al., 2016; Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The expression levels of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C were significantly lower in kinase-type PCC cells than in metabolism-type PCC cells.
claims.source: the expression levels of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C were significantly lower in kinase-type PCC cells than in metabolism-type PCC cells (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Immunohistochemistry staining showed lower expression of HLA-A in P4 compared to other patients.
claims.source: Consistently, immunohistochemistry staining of serial sections of tumor tissues showed lower expression of HLA-A in P4 as compared to that in other patients (Figure 7C)
claims.evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Eight immune cell types were identified including central memory CD4+ T cells, effector memory CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer T cells, natural killer cells, B cells, M1 macrophages, and M2 macrophages.
claims.source: We additionally assessed the immune microenvironment of PCCs by subclustering immunotherapy-related immune cells and identified eight clusters including central memory CD4+ T cells (CD4+ TCM, marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, CCR7, and IL7R), effector memory CD4+ T cells (CD4+ TEM, marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, and IL7R), CD8+ T cells (marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD8A and CD8B), natural killer T cells (NKTs, marked by CD3E, KLRD1 and GNLY), natural killer cells (NKs, marked by KLRD1 and GNLY), B cells (marked by MS4A1 and CD79A), M1 macrophages (marked by CD68), and M2 macrophages (marked by CD68 and CD163) (Figure 7D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by marker gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claims.claim: The proportion of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages increased in tumor tissues compared with adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues.
claims.source: Further analysis of immune cell type composition in metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs showed an increase in the proportion of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages in tumor tissues as compared with that in adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues
claims.evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The proportion of M2 macrophages decreased in tumor tissues compared with adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues.
claims.source: while the proportion of M2 macrophages in adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues decreased as compared with that in tumor tissues (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: CD8+ T cells play an essential role in anti-tumor immunity by recognizing tumor antigens displayed on the surface of tumor cells by HLA-I molecules.
claims.source: In particular, the CD8+ T cells play an essential role in anti-tumor immunity; these cells can recognize tumor antigens displayed on the surface of tumor cells by HLA-I molecules (Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021).

claims.claim: CD8+ T cells were rare and only present in tumor stroma of P1-P5.
claims.source: We observed that CD8+ T cells, as well as CD4+ T cells, M1 macrophages, and M2 macrophages were rare (and were only present in tumor stroma of P1-P5), indicating apparent immune escape in both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: Supported by multispectral immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Kinases such as RET, ALK, and MEK have negative regulatory effects on HLA-I expression on tumor cells.
claims.source: Combined with previously reported negative regulatory effects of kinases (such as RET, ALK, and MEK) on HLA-I expression on tumor cells (Brea et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Brea et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The possible reason for inability in recruiting CD8+ T cells of kinase-type PCCs is the down-regulation of HLA-I in tumor cells regulated by RET.
claims.source: we speculate that the possible reason for inability in recruiting CD8+ T cells of kinase-type PCCs is the down-regulation of HLA-I in tumor cells regulated by RET
claims.evidence: Speculative claim based on observed HLA-I downregulation and prior literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I.

claims.claim: RET inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with RET mutation.
claims.source: Recently, RET inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with RET mutation (Drilon et al., 2020; Griesinger et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drilon et al., 2020; Griesinger et al., 2022).

claims.claim: 40~50% of PCCs have been classified into a certain molecular pathway (pseudohypoxia, kinase, or Wnt).
claims.source: According to the results of genomics research in recent years, 40~50% of PCCs have been classified into a certain molecular pathway (pseudohypoxia, kinase, or Wnt), but the remaining 50–60% are still unclassified (Crona et al., 2017; Lenders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Crona et al., 2017; Lenders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Isotope therapies can only relieve the clinical symptoms in 50% of patients without reducing tumor size.
claims.source: Isotope therapies can only relieve the clinical symptoms in 50% of patients (without reducing tumor size; Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Roman-Gonzalez and Jimenez, 2017)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Roman-Gonzalez and Jimenez, 2017).

claims.claim: Most chemotherapies and targeted therapies exhibit low remission rates and severe side effects in clinical studies for PCCs.
claims.source: while most chemotherapies and targeted therapies exhibit low remission rates and severe side effects in clinical studies (Druce et al., 2009; Hamidi, 2019; O'Kane et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Druce et al., 2009; Hamidi, 2019; O'Kane et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2012).

claims.claim: One clinical trial investigating ICIs for metastatic PCCs showed 43% non-progression rate (NPR) and 0% overall response rate (ORR) in seven PCC patients.
claims.source: Currently, there are only two clinical trials investigating the efficacy of ICIs for the treatment of metastatic PCCs: one is still in the recruitment stage, and the other showed 43% non-progression rate (NPR) and 0% overall response rate (ORR) in seven PCC patients (Dai et al., 2020; Jimenez et al., 2022; Naing et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Dai et al., 2020; Jimenez et al., 2022; Naing et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The PASS scoring system is weighted for histologic features and has been used to separate tumors with potential for biologically aggressive behavior (PASS ≥ 4) from tumors with benign lesion (PASS < 4).
claims.source: A scoring system—the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS)—is weighted for histologic features and has been used to separate tumors with a potential for a biologically aggressive behavior (PASS > or = 4) from tumors with benign lesion (PASS < 4) (Thompson, 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Thompson, 2002).

claims.claim: The utility of PASS scoring system is restricted due to observer variation and nonrepeatability.
claims.source: Although the PASS scoring system was proposed as a tool for discriminating potentially metastasis PCCs from benign ones, its utility is somewhat restricted due to observer variation and nonrepeatability (Agarwal et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 2014; Thompson, 2002; Wu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Agarwal et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 2014; Thompson, 2002; Wu et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Whole exome sequencing of sporadic PCC tumor tissues detected somatic mutations in JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, and MST1.
claims.source: Four of these patients (P1-P4) suffered from sporadic PCCs: whole exome sequencing (WES) of these tumor tissues detected somatic mutations as compared with their adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues, including in JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, and MST1 (Supplementary file 1a)
claims.evidence: Supported by WES data in Supplementary file 1a.

claims.claim: P5 had a germline missense mutation in VHL.
claims.source: The cohort also included 1 hereditary PCC patient (P5) with Type 2 Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, with a germline missense mutation in VHL (Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: Supported by WES data in Supplementary file 1a.

claims.claim: PCC cells show typical cell arrangement (small alveoli surrounded by fibro-vascular stroma) and characteristic shapes (polygonal or fusiform cells).
claims.source: The morphology of PCC cells was assessed through hematoxylin-eosin-stained tumor tissues, showing the typical cell arrangement (small alveoli surrounded by fibro-vascular stroma) and characteristic shapes (polygonal or fusiform cells) of PCCs (Lupşan et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior literature (Lupşan et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Immunocytochemistry staining showed robust expression of Chromogranin A (CGA) in PCC tumor tissues.
claims.source: Meanwhile, immunocytochemistry staining showed robust expression of Chromogranin A (CGA) in these tumor tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Inferred diploid normal cells expressing high levels of CYP17A1 and HSD3B2 were defined as adrenocortical cells.
claims.source: The inferred diploid normal cells expressing high levels of CYP17A1 and HSD3B2 were defined as adrenocortical cells (Kubota-Nakayama et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature (Kubota-Nakayama et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Inferred diploid normal cells showing low CHGB expression were defined as normal chromaffin cells.
claims.source: while the inferred diploid normal cells showing low CHGB expression were defined as normal chromaffin cells (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: A cluster of inferred diploid normal cells with high expression of VWF was found in the VHL patient (P5).
claims.source: We also found a cluster of inferred diploid normal cells with high expression of VWF (a marker for vascular endothelial cells) in the VHL patient (P5) (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: Metabolism-type PCCs correspond to the pseudo-hypoxic type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
claims.source: These results support that the previously unclassified PCCs can be classified as metabolism-type or kinase-type based on transcriptional programs, with these types partially corresponding to the pseudo-hypoxic type and kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the molecular characteristics and comparison with TCGA classification.

claims.claim: Kinase-type PCCs correspond to the kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
claims.source: These results support that the previously unclassified PCCs can be classified as metabolism-type or kinase-type based on transcriptional programs, with these types partially corresponding to the pseudo-hypoxic type and kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the molecular characteristics and comparison with TCGA classification.

claims.claim: Kinase-signaling PCCs by TCGA classification include germline and somatic mutations in RET and are uniquely able to secrete epinephrine owing to their high expression of PNMT.
claims.source: Consistently, kinase-signaling PCCs by TCGA classification include germline and somatic mutations in RET, and are uniquely able to secrete epinephrine, owing to their high expression of PNMT
claims.evidence: Draws from established knowledge about TCGA classification of PCCs.

claims.claim: P5 displays reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism caused by VHL mutation and subsequent HIF dysregulation.
claims.source: P5 could also be classified into the metabolism-type we defined, which is known to display reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism caused by VHL mutation and subsequent HIF dysregulation (Chappell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Chappell et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Subcluster 2 of metabolism-type PCCs has higher metastasis potential compared with subcluster 1.
claims.source: Late up-regulated genes include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion, which highly expressed in subcluster 2 (Figure 5C), suggesting the higher metastasis potential of subcluster 2 as compared with subcluster 1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the expression of metastasis-promoting genes in subcluster 2.

claims.claim: The major clone in kinase-type PCCs has changed from subcluster 1 to subcluster 2 along the trajectory.
claims.source: We then clustered kinase-type PCC cells into two subclusters and found that the major clone has been changed from subcluster 1–2 along the trajectory (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: VEGF pathway activation is consistent with vascular endothelial hyperplasia caused by VHL mutation in VHL syndrome.
claims.source: The observed activation of VEGF pathway is consistent with the vascular endothelial hyperplasia caused by VHL mutation in VHL syndrome (Vortmeyer et al., 2013) and the elevated proportion of endothelial cells in this patient (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Vortmeyer et al., 2013) and cell type composition data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs mediate tumor angiogenesis and metastasis in P5.
claims.source: Specifically, VEGFA and VEGFR1 were highly expressed in tumor cells, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 in endothelial cells, and PLGF in fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 6G), suggesting the crosstalk between tumor cells and fibroblasts or endothelial cells in tumor microenvironment through these ligand-receptor pairs, which mediated in the tumor angiogenesis and metastasis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the expression patterns of ligands and receptors and established knowledge about VEGF pathway function.

claims.claim: FGF1-FGFR1 pair regulates tumor cell proliferation through cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells.
claims.source: The analyses suggested the cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells through the FGF1-FGFR1 pair, which regulated the tumor cell proliferation (Katoh, 2016).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the expression patterns of FGF1 and FGFR1 and supported by citation to prior literature (Katoh, 2016).

claims.source: These results indicate that kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors, which have been shown to exert inhibitory effects on tumor proliferation (Liang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2012).

claims.source: while the mechanism of immune escape in metabolism-type PCCs (with antigen presentation ability) needs to be further explored.
claims.evidence: Acknowledged gap in understanding based on the observed immune escape despite antigen presentation ability.

claims.claim: RET inhibitors may enhance the antigen presentation ability of tumor cells in kinase-type PCCs.
claims.source: For kinase-type PCCs, whether RET inhibitors can enhance the antigen presentation ability of tumor cells, and further provide chance for combination of kinase-targeted therapy and immunotherapy, needs to be verified by follow-up research.
claims.evidence: Speculative claim requiring future verification.

claims.source: Despite the patient cohort in our study including a hereditary PCC patient, only one patient with a VHL germline mutation was included; other types of hereditary PCCs with germline mutations (for example in SDHx and FH) were not included.
claims.evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.

claims.source: In addition, the specimens were all from primary tumors, while no metastatic tumors were included.
claims.evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.

claims.source: The number of sporadic cases was also limited, mainly caused by the low incidence of PCCs.
claims.evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.

results.result: PCCs are rare neuroendocrine tumors originating from adrenal chromaffin cells with diverse driver alterations. Despite molecular classification efforts, 50-60% remain unclassified, and all PCCs are now considered malignant with metastatic potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by citations to established literature. These claims provide essential background context about PCC biology, classification challenges, and clinical significance, forming the foundation for the study's rationale.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of 133,894 cells from PCC specimens identified 13 distinct cell types in the tumor microenvironment, with pathological validation confirming PCC characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 and C81-C82 are supported by scRNA-seq data processing, marker gene expression analysis, and histological/immunohistochemical validation. The cell type identification using established markers and correlation analysis is methodologically sound.

results.result: Intra-tumoral heterogeneity was less extensive than inter-individual heterogeneity in PCCs, with distinct cellular composition patterns distinguishing patients despite variable PASS scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C19-C22 are supported by correlation analysis and cell type composition data. The finding that scRNA-seq reveals different heterogeneity patterns than PASS scoring is well-documented with quantitative evidence from Figures 2A-D.

results.result: CopyKAT algorithm successfully distinguished tumor cells from normal cells based on CNV patterns, identifying two distinct tumor clusters with different chromosomal alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 and C83-C85 are supported by CNV analysis and marker gene expression validation. The use of CopyKAT is appropriately cited and the distinction between aneuploid tumor cells and diploid normal cells is validated by marker expression.

results.result: Unclassified PCCs were divided into metabolism-type (marked by NDUFA4L2/COX4I2) and kinase-type (marked by RET/PNMT) based on gene expression and CNV patterns, validated by immunohistochemistry and corresponding to TCGA classifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C27-C35 are well-supported by scRNA-seq data, GO enrichment analysis, and protein-level validation. The classification is biologically coherent with established knowledge (C29-C31) and appropriately linked to TCGA categories (C86-C87). However, the sample size is limited (n=4 sporadic, n=1 VHL).

results.result: Clinical and molecular features of kinase-type PCCs align with TCGA kinase-signaling classification, showing elevated catecholamine metabolites and PNMT expression. The VHL patient displays metabolic reprogramming consistent with metabolism-type classification.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C88-C89 are supported by clinical data and literature citations. The correlation between molecular classification and clinical phenotype strengthens the validity of the proposed classification scheme.

results.result: Trajectory analysis revealed that metabolism-type PCCs display consistently active metabolism with increasing metastasis potential over tumor evolution, marked by early expression of metabolic genes and late upregulation of invasion-promoting genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C37-C40 are supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis. The progression from tumor suppressor (SPINT2) to oncogene (JUNB) expression and upregulation of EMT markers (S100A4, TAGLN) provides coherent evidence for increased metastatic potential. Claim C90 appropriately infers higher metastatic potential from gene expression patterns.

results.result: Kinase-type PCCs showed decreased epinephrine synthesis and acquisition of neuron-like phenotypes during evolution, with clonal shift from subcluster 1 to 2 and late RET upregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C41-C45 are supported by pseudotime analysis and validated by prior literature on RET-associated neuron-like phenotypes. The temporal dynamics of PNMT (early) versus neuron-specific genes (late) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 5F.

results.result: Metabolism-type PCCs exhibit activation of the annexin pathway (primarily ANXA1-FPR1) and strong inflammatory response, with elevated neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C46-C50 are supported by CellChat analysis, GSEA enrichment, and cell composition data. The connection between annexin pathway activation and inflammatory response is well-established in cited literature (C48), and the elevated immune cell proportions provide mechanistic support.

results.result: The VHL patient (P5) showed VEGF pathway activation through PLGF-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR1/2 pairs, consistent with vascular endothelial hyperplasia characteristic of VHL syndrome.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C51-C53 are supported by CellChat analysis and gene expression data. The consistency with known VHL syndrome phenotype (C92) and elevated endothelial cell proportion strengthens the finding. Claim C93 appropriately infers functional consequences from expression patterns and established pathway knowledge.

results.result: Kinase-type PCCs display FGF signaling activation through FGF1-FGFR1 interactions among tumor, stromal, and immune cells, regulating tumor proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C54-C57 are supported by CellChat analysis and expression data. The cell-cell communication inference is appropriately validated by literature citation (C57). Claim C94 reasonably infers functional significance from expression patterns and prior knowledge.

results.result: Kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors based on FGF pathway activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is speculative and based solely on pathway activation without functional validation. While C95 cites literature supporting FGFR inhibitor effects on proliferation, no experimental evidence is provided for PCCs specifically. This therapeutic suggestion requires validation in follow-up studies.

results.result: Both PCC types lack CD8+ T cell infiltration, but only kinase-type PCCs show downregulated HLA-I expression, suggesting distinct immune escape mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C59-C64 are supported by multispectral immunofluorescence, scRNA-seq expression analysis, and immunohistochemistry. The differential HLA-I expression between types is well-documented. Claim C61 appropriately infers immune evasion from lack of tumor-T cell communication, though the mechanism requires further investigation.

results.result: Eight immune cell types were identified with altered proportions in tumor versus normal tissue. CD8+ T cells were rare and restricted to tumor stroma, indicating immune escape in both PCC types.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by marker-based cell type identification and multispectral immunofluorescence validation. The spatial restriction of CD8+ T cells to stroma (not tumor parenchyma) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7G, providing strong evidence for immune escape.

results.result: Kinase-type PCCs exhibit HLA-I downregulation possibly regulated by RET, based on co-expression patterns and prior literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I.
results.evaluation: Claim C13 is supported by expression and IHC data, but C14 and C71 are speculative. While C70 cites literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I, the direct regulatory relationship between RET and HLA-I in PCCs is not experimentally validated. The correlation is suggestive but requires functional validation.

results.result: Kinase-type PCCs have potential for combined kinase inhibitor and immunotherapy based on HLA-I downregulation and RET expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C15 and C97 are speculative therapeutic suggestions without experimental validation. While C72 establishes RET inhibitor approval for other cancers, the efficacy in PCCs and potential synergy with immunotherapy remain unproven. This requires clinical validation as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Immunotherapy application to metabolism-type PCCs is likely unsuitable despite antigen presentation ability, though the immune escape mechanism requires further exploration.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 is speculative based on lack of CD8+ T cell infiltration despite HLA-I expression. The paradox of antigen presentation without T cell recruitment (C96) indicates incomplete mechanistic understanding. The therapeutic conclusion is premature without understanding the escape mechanism.

results.result: Current PCC classification systems leave 50-60% unclassified, and existing therapies show limited efficacy with low response rates and significant limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are well-supported by citations to prior literature, establishing the clinical need for improved classification and therapeutic strategies. These claims provide important context for the study's significance.

results.result: Whole exome sequencing identified somatic mutations in sporadic PCCs (JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, MST1) and germline VHL mutation in the hereditary case.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by WES data in supplementary files. The mutations identified do not fit established TCGA categories, justifying the focus on unclassified PCCs.

results.result: Study limitations include single VHL patient, no other hereditary types, no metastatic tumors, and limited sporadic cases due to low PCC incidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are appropriately acknowledged limitations by the authors. These constraints affect generalizability and highlight the need for larger, more diverse cohorts in future studies.

results.result: The authors classified previously unclassified PCCs into two subtypes based on scRNA-seq: metabolism-type (marked by NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2, enriched for metabolic pathways) and kinase-type (marked by RET and PNMT, enriched for kinase signaling and neuron development). This classification was validated by immunohistochemistry and corresponds partially to TCGA pseudo-hypoxic and kinase-signaling types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognized this as a main finding, with one reviewer stating the authors 'defined "metabolism-type" and "kinase-type" in unclassified sporadic PCC patients through single-cell transcriptomics-based differentially expressed genes and functional enrichment analyses.' The editor noted the authors 'propose a new molecular classification criterion based on solid evidence.' No concerns were raised about the validity of this classification.

results.result: Trajectory analysis revealed that metabolism-type PCC cells display consistently active metabolism and increased metastasis potential, with late upregulation of metastasis-promoting genes (S100A4, TAGLN) and oncogene JUNB, while early expressing metabolism genes (NDUFA4L2, ATP5MG) and tumor suppressor SPINT2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the trajectory analysis findings without raising concerns. One reviewer noted the study 'validated the scRNA-seq analysis results' with immunocytochemistry. The trajectory analysis is presented as supporting evidence for the molecular classification and was not questioned.

results.result: Kinase-type PCC cells showed decreased epinephrine synthesis and neuron-like phenotypes during tumor evolution, with early expression of CALM1/CALM2 and PNMT, followed by late upregulation of RET and neuron-specific genes (MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, CNTN1).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these trajectory findings as part of the characterization of kinase-type PCCs. One reviewer explicitly mentioned the study's findings about 'neuron-like phenotypes' without criticism. The consistency with prior literature on RET-expressing PCCs was noted in the manuscript and not challenged.

results.result: Cell-cell communication analysis showed activation of the annexin pathway (via ANXA1-FPR1) and strong inflammatory response in metabolism-type PCCs, with higher proportions of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages compared to kinase-type.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these cell-cell communication findings. The characterization of the tumor microenvironment was recognized as a strength, with the editor noting the work 'advances our understanding' based on 'characterization of tumor microenvironmental features.' No methodological concerns were raised about the CellChat analysis.

results.result: FGF signaling (via FGF1-FGFR1) is activated in kinase-type PCCs through cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma, and immune cells, regulating tumor proliferation. The authors suggest kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the FGF signaling findings without criticism. The therapeutic suggestion about FGFR inhibitors was not challenged, though it is speculative. The cell-cell communication analysis was validated alongside other findings and considered part of the solid evidence base.

results.result: VEGF signaling pathway is activated in the VHL patient (P5) through PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1, and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs, consistent with vascular endothelial hyperplasia in VHL syndrome and mediating tumor angiogenesis and metastasis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these findings specific to the VHL patient. The consistency with known VHL syndrome phenotypes strengthens the claim. The characterization of this hereditary case was accepted as part of the overall tumor microenvironment analysis.

results.result: Both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs lack CD8+ T cell infiltration (confirmed by multispectral immunofluorescence), but only kinase-type PCCs exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C), validated by immunohistochemistry showing lower HLA-A expression in P4.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognized this as a main finding, with one stating the study 'revealed a lack of immune cell infiltration in both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs, while only the kinase-type PCC patient exhibited the low expression of HLA-I.' The validation with immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry was noted as a strength.

results.result: HLA-I downregulation in kinase-type PCCs is possibly regulated by RET, based on co-occurrence and prior literature showing kinases (RET, ALK, MEK) negatively regulate HLA-I expression. This is proposed as the mechanism for inability to recruit CD8+ T cells in kinase-type PCCs.
results.evaluation: One reviewer criticized this interpretation as 'rather one-sided,' noting that 'the low number of infiltrating T cells in tumor tissue may be influenced by a variety of factors, such as the release of catecholamines, the expression of inhibitory receptors on the surface of T cells, and so on, although genetic mutation still plays the most crucial role.' The reviewer requested updated references and expanded discussion, indicating the mechanistic claim is insufficiently supported.

results.result: The authors suggest kinase-type PCCs have potential for combined therapy with kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy (based on HLA-I downregulation by RET), while immunotherapy is likely unsuitable for metabolism-type PCCs despite their antigen presentation ability. The mechanism of immune escape in metabolism-type PCCs needs further exploration.
results.evaluation: One reviewer found the therapeutic conclusions 'rather one-sided' and noted the discussion 'needs to be updated or corrected and expanded.' The reviewer emphasized that immune escape mechanisms are complex and multifactorial. While reviewers acknowledged these as potential therapeutic implications, the insufficient mechanistic understanding and outdated literature base undermine confidence in these speculative claims.

results.result: The PASS scores of collected PCC tissues ranged from 2 to 9, showing heterogeneity. The authors used PASS scoring to assess tumor aggressiveness, though the system has limitations including observer variation and nonrepeatability.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raised significant concerns about the use of PASS scoring, noting that 'multiparametric scoring systems such as PASS are no longer endorsed in the 2022 WHO guidelines' and questioning why PASS was chosen over GAPP, m-GAPP, or COPPS. The reviewer requested the authors 'emphasize the importance and necessity of using the PASS scoring system' or consider removing this content as it 'does not seem to be very relevant to the subject of the article.' The editor also noted the work 'could be improved further through delineating the choice of the PASS scoring system.'

results.result: Intra-tumoral heterogeneity was less extensive than inter-individual heterogeneity. P4 showed low correlation with other sporadic PCCs (P1-P3) and had elevated adrenal cells (77% vs 16-36%). P5 had higher endothelial cells (35% vs 3-10%).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these heterogeneity findings without criticism. One reviewer noted the study 'described the intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity by performing scRNA-seq.' The characterization of patient-specific differences was recognized as part of the solid evidence base.

results.result: After quality control, 133,894 cells were retained and classified into 13 cell types using marker genes. CopyKAT algorithm distinguished PCC cells from normal chromaffin cells based on CNVs, with aneuploid tumor cells highly expressing CHGB. Two CNV patterns were identified with distinctions in chromosomes 3, 11, and 17.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the technical quality of the scRNA-seq data or cell type identification. One reviewer noted the 'article is logically written and the results are clearly presented.' The methodology was accepted as sound, with validation through marker gene expression and immunostaining noted as a strength.

results.result: Cell-cell communication analysis showed apparent crosstalk between tumor cells and T cells in metabolism-type patients, but lack of communication in kinase-type patient, suggesting kinase-type PCC cells could evade immune surveillance of T cells.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge the CellChat findings, one reviewer criticized the overall interpretation of immune escape mechanisms as 'rather one-sided' and noted multiple factors influence T cell infiltration. The inference about immune evasion specifically through lack of communication is part of the broader mechanistic interpretation that reviewers found insufficiently supported.

results.result: Eight immune cell types were identified including CD4+ T cell subsets, CD8+ T cells, NKTs, NKs, B cells, and M1/M2 macrophages. CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages increased in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues, while M2 macrophages decreased.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the immune cell characterization without criticism. One reviewer noted the study 'validated the scRNA-seq analysis results (such as the expression levels of marker genes and the distribution of immune cells in the PCC microenvironment) with immunocytochemistry and multispectral immunofluorescent staining' as a strength.

results.result: WES detected somatic mutations in JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, and MST1 in sporadic PCCs (P1-P4), and P5 had a germline VHL mutation. Study limitations include only one VHL patient, no metastatic tumors, and limited sporadic cases due to low PCC incidence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the genomic characterization or acknowledged limitations. The study design limitations were transparently reported by the authors and accepted by reviewers as inherent constraints given the rarity of PCCs.

results.result: Background and contextual claims about PCCs, including their origin, molecular diversity, classification challenges, malignant potential, treatment limitations, and established biological knowledge about marker genes, pathways, and cell types.
results.evaluation: These are background claims supported by citations to prior literature or established knowledge. Reviewers did not question these foundational statements, though one reviewer noted the references are dated (mostly 2021 and earlier) and requested comprehensive updates to the literature, particularly regarding immune microenvironment characterization.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the metabolism-type and kinase-type molecular classification (C6, C27-C35, C86-C87). OpenEval notes the classification is biologically coherent with appropriate validation but mentions limited sample size. Peer reviewers explicitly recognized this as a main finding based on 'solid evidence' without raising concerns about the classification validity.

Perfect agreement on trajectory analysis findings (C7, C37-C40, C90). Both evaluations support the progression from tumor suppressor to oncogene expression and increased metastatic potential. OpenEval provides detailed methodological validation; peer reviewers accepted these findings without criticism as supporting evidence for molecular classification.

Complete agreement on neuron-like phenotype trajectory findings (C8, C41-C45, C91). Both evaluations support the temporal dynamics and consistency with RET-associated literature. OpenEval emphasizes validation by prior literature; peer reviewers explicitly mentioned neuron-like phenotypes without criticism.

Full agreement on annexin pathway and inflammatory response findings (C9-C10, C46-C50). Both evaluations support the CellChat analysis and tumor microenvironment characterization. OpenEval validates mechanistic connections; peer reviewers recognized this as advancing understanding without methodological concerns.

Both support FGF signaling findings (C11, C54-C57, C94), but differ on therapeutic speculation (C58, C95). OpenEval rates C58 and C95 as UNCERTAIN requiring validation. Peer reviewers accepted the FGF findings and did not challenge the FGFR inhibitor suggestion, though it remains speculative.

Strong agreement on VHL patient findings (C51-C53, C92-C93). Both evaluations support the cell-cell communication analysis and consistency with known VHL syndrome phenotypes. OpenEval notes appropriate inference from expression patterns; peer reviewers accepted this as part of solid tumor microenvironment analysis.

Both support differential HLA-I expression findings (C12, C63-C64, C69). OpenEval notes the data is well-documented but immune evasion mechanism requires further investigation. Peer reviewers explicitly recognized lack of immune infiltration and low HLA-I in kinase-type as a main finding with validation noted as strength.

Both rate RET-HLA-I regulatory relationship as UNCERTAIN (C14, C70-C71). OpenEval notes the correlation is suggestive but requires functional validation. Peer reviewers criticized this interpretation as 'rather one-sided,' emphasizing multiple factors influence T cell infiltration and requesting expanded discussion with updated references.

Both rate therapeutic conclusions as UNCERTAIN (C15-C16, C96-C97). OpenEval notes speculation without experimental validation and incomplete mechanistic understanding. Peer reviewers found therapeutic conclusions 'rather one-sided' with insufficient mechanistic support and outdated literature, requesting updates and expanded discussion.

Both support heterogeneity findings (C5, C20-C22). OpenEval validates that scRNA-seq reveals different patterns than PASS scoring with quantitative evidence. Peer reviewers accepted the intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity characterization as part of solid evidence base without criticism.

Divergent evaluations on PASS scoring relevance (C19, C77-C78). OpenEval supports the comparison between scRNA-seq and PASS as methodologically sound. Peer reviewers raised significant concerns that PASS is no longer endorsed in 2022 WHO guidelines, questioning its necessity and relevance to the article's subject.

Both support cell type identification methodology (C17-C18). OpenEval validates scRNA-seq data processing and marker gene analysis as methodologically sound. Peer reviewers accepted technical quality without questioning, noting logical presentation and clear results with validation through immunostaining.

Both support CNV analysis and tumor cell identification (C24-C26, C83-C85). OpenEval validates CopyKAT usage and marker expression validation. Peer reviewers accepted methodology as sound without questioning technical quality of cell type identification.

Partial agreement on immune evasion findings (C59-C61). OpenEval supports the data but notes immune evasion inference requires further investigation. Peer reviewers did not directly challenge CellChat findings but criticized the broader interpretation of immune escape mechanisms as 'rather one-sided' with multiple influencing factors.

Complete agreement on spatial immune cell distribution (C65-C67). Both evaluations strongly support the finding that CD8+ T cells are restricted to stroma. OpenEval emphasizes clear demonstration in immunofluorescence; peer reviewers noted validation of immune cell distribution as a strength.

Both support study limitations and genomic characterization (C79-C80, C98-C100). OpenEval notes these are appropriately acknowledged constraints affecting generalizability. Peer reviewers accepted transparent reporting of limitations and did not question genomic characterization or inherent constraints given PCC rarity.

Both support background and contextual claims (C1-C4). OpenEval validates these are well-supported by established literature providing essential rationale. Peer reviewers did not question foundational statements, though noted references are dated and requested comprehensive literature updates.

Both support clinical context claims (C73-C78). OpenEval validates these establish clinical need through prior literature citations. Peer reviewers accepted these background claims without questioning, though requested updated references particularly for immune microenvironment characterization.

Both support clinical phenotype correlation (C36, C88-C89). OpenEval notes this strengthens the molecular classification validity. Peer reviewers accepted these established knowledge claims without criticism as part of background literature.

OpenEval rates FGFR inhibitor therapeutic suggestion (C58, C95) as UNCERTAIN requiring validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the speculative nature of this therapeutic claim, though peer R5 accepted FGF signaling findings without challenging the inhibitor suggestion.

OpenEval rates immune checkpoint therapy suggestion (C16, C96) as UNCERTAIN due to paradox of HLA-I expression without T cell recruitment. While peer R9 addresses therapeutic conclusions broadly, no specific peer evaluation focuses on this particular mechanistic paradox and its implications for checkpoint therapy.

OpenEval supports WES mutation findings (C79-C80) justifying focus on unclassified PCCs. While peer R15 accepts genomic characterization, no peer evaluation specifically validates the WES data showing mutations don't fit established TCGA categories.
